drills.q: Give the time split for a STAR answer, in percentages and seconds.
drills.a: S 10% ~15s, T 10% ~15s, A 50% ~90s, R 15% ~25s, rejected alternative 10% ~20s, redo 5% ~10s. Candidates invert it by spending most of the answer on Situation.

drills.q: How many sentences is the 60-second version, and what happens next?
drills.a: Nine: 1 Situation, 1 Task, 3 Action, 1 Result, 1 rejected alternative. Then stop and offer a direction. The 3-minute version is never given unprompted.

drills.q: The interviewer says 'tell me about the hardest bug you've debugged.' Which story, and what is the opening sentence?
drills.a: The OOM on 1.2M multilingual rows. Open on the symptom: the process was killed with no Python traceback, which is the kernel OOM killer rather than an application exception.

drills.q: Why not just raise the memory limit on the embedding job?
drills.a: Peak memory scaled with corpus size rather than batch size, because the whole ClickHouse result set was materialised into Python objects. Raising the limit relocates the failure to the next growth step, and the corpus grows by design.

drills.q: Is gc.collect() at page boundaries a good fix? Defend or concede.
drills.a: Concede: it compensates for CPython allocator and cycle-collector behaviour rather than removing the cause. The structural fix is streaming with generators and bounded batches. Placement still mattered: inside the hot loop it would destroy throughput; at page boundaries the pause amortises over thousands of rows.

drills.q: Defend the ~25% engagement uplift. What must your answer contain, in order?
drills.a: Metric definition first, comparison design second (holdout vs staged rollout vs pre/post), confounders you could not remove third. Volunteer the method before being asked. If it was pre/post, say so and name why a holdout was unavailable. Never claim a controlled experiment you did not run.

drills.q: 'Why eight services and not one?' Answer in three moves.
drills.a: 1) Name the criterion: independent scaling and independent failure, not data entities; three profiles diverge (latency-bound serving, throughput-bound ingestion, batch processing). 2) State the real cost before they do: eight pipelines, eight dashboard sets, distributed tracing needed to answer one user question. 3) Volunteer the merge: at least two would be merged today, because services that always change and deploy together are one service plus a network hop.

drills.q: Why was patching only the endpoints you found the wrong fix for the cross-tenant authz bypass, and why is middleware insufficient?
drills.a: The class of bug is authorization decided per endpoint; fixing instances leaves the class. Middleware sees the route and the token but generally cannot see which object IDs the handler is about to load, so enforcement belongs on the object-fetch path keyed on the authenticated tenant. The design fix behind the code fix: make tenant identity a required non-defaultable parameter rather than a convention.

drills.q: Someone assumes you dropped functionality going from 3,447 Java lines to 812 Python lines. Respond.
drills.a: Most of the Java was Spring Batch scaffolding: item readers, writers, processors, job and step configuration. The transformation rules were a small fraction of it. The new service also added explicit multi-tenant isolation the old one lacked.

drills.q: Why a contextual bandit rather than a gradient-boosted ranker, and what was missing from your evaluation?
drills.a: A ranker trained on logged clicks learns the previous policy's preferences, so unseen content is never shown and never generates the data that would justify showing it; offline replay cannot detect this because it scores against the logged policy. Missing: off-policy evaluation via inverse propensity scoring, which meant policy changes were effectively live experiments.

drills.q: 'Tell me about a time you failed.' Give the story and the one thing your answer must contain.
drills.a: The over-decomposition of the platform (or the knowledge-graph attribution gap: shipped alongside content embeddings, contribution never isolated). It must contain a COST: extra deploy overhead, a component you cannot justify, time spent. A failure with no cost is not a failure.

drills.q: 'Tell me about a time you disagreed.' What is the follow-up you must be able to survive?
drills.a: 'Tell me about a time you disagreed and were WRONG.' Without it, every disagreement story reads as 'I was right and they came around'. Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit is two clauses and most candidates evidence only the first.

drills.q: How do the MongoDB race and the async event loop error differ in cause, and what were the wrong fixes?
drills.a: Race: read-modify-write across a network round trip is not atomic; wrong fix is app-level locking (serialises the hot path), right fix is an atomic update operator with a filter condition. Loop error: a client created on one event loop used from another, or a module-level client outliving its loop; wrong fix is broad try/except (converts a correctness bug to a silent one), right fix is loop-scoped client lifecycle tied to startup and shutdown. Both are invisible at parallelism one, which is what most test suites use.

drills.q: Name the six stories you cannot enter a senior loop without.
drills.a: Disagreed and was wrong. A real failure with a real cost. Said no and lost. Influenced without authority. Reframed a wrong requirement. Prevented an expensive mistake.

drills.q: The write-up says 'insufficient evidence of impact beyond own team.' Which stories fix this, and what makes them work?
drills.a: The credential mechanism adopted across a service fleet, Query Crafter unblocking non-technical stakeholders in other functions, the Credit Suisse automation done from a Business Analyst seat, and the Skillmaster integration into another team's provisioning platform. What makes them work is naming which teams and what the coordination actually was, rather than inflating single-team work.

drills.q: Why must golden-baseline assertions be aggregate rather than exact-match?
drills.a: A semantic system that must return byte-identical output cannot be improved. Separate 'must never change' (locale precedence, tenant scoping, pagination: exact) from 'may drift within tolerance' (resolutions, rankings: aggregate with tolerance bands). A new embedding model changes every vector but should be a no-op at the assertion level if resolution decisions are preserved.
